newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania reorients foreign policy to win NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Romania reorients foreign policy to win NATO entry.

text.p: Romania, seeking to boost its chances of early admission to NATO, wants to develop a new partnership with Hungary and Poland and has put improved ties with Ukraine at the top of its foreign policy agenda.
"There's a different tune in our foreign policy," Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told Reuters on the eve of a 24-hour visit by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
Rifkind meets Romania's new leadership on Tuesday, including President Emil Constantinescu and Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, before travelling on to Bulgaria.
Severin praised Britain's "open, pragmatic stance" on Romania's determination to gain early NATO membership against odds favouring more advanced candidates Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

"Western diplomats are telling us that we are now moving at top speed, rather than the previous snail's pace," said Severin, a member of the centrist coalition which ousted leftists at general and presidential elections two months ago.

France last week assured Romania that it would support the ex-communist country's bid to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as the alliance goes ahead with its eastward expansion plans at a July summit in Madrid.
Bucharest expects French President Jacques Chirac to reinforce that support when he visits Romania next month.
"The idea of a strategic partnership with Poland and Hungary has been accepted in principle," Severin said. "We have to put it into effect quickly."
Severin visited Budapest last month and accompanied Constantinescu to Warsaw in the New Year.

Romanian and Hungarian diplomats resume talks in Budapest in mid-February on implementing a treaty signed last year, which buried old rifts between the two ex-communist neighbours over borders and treatment of ethnic minorities.

Severin singled out the creation of a Romanian-Hungarian military unit, patterned on the post-war Franco-German model, as part of accords to be signed next month by defence, transport and interior ministers.
Changing priorities after the 1989 fall of communism, Romania also wants to improve ties with neighbouring ex-Soviet Ukraine.
"Romania has a strategic interest in the consolidation of Ukraine's independence and statehood," Severin said.

Talks on a long-delayed political treaty resumed this month with both sides trying to overcome the main snag -- Bucharest's insistence that Ukraine atone for the loss of Romanian lands to Moscow under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact.
Similar treaties remain unsigned with Russia and ex-Soviet Moldova, mainly for the same reasons.
Russia last week repeated its opposition to NATO expansion during a visit to Moscow by the alliance's chief, Javier Solana.
Ukraine has no plans to join, but voices no objections to enlargement and is nurturing close ties with the alliance.
